en.title: Diablo Creator David Brevik Names the 'Worst Game Ending' He's Ever Played
en.summary: The legendary designer behind Diablo, David Brevik, has revealed his pick for the worst game ending in history. Despite his own celebrated career, Brevik finds one particular conclusion to be a major letdown.
en.body:
## A Legendary Critic's Disappointment

**David Brevik**, the visionary game designer who brought us the iconic **Diablo**, has spoken out about what he considers the absolute worst game ending he has ever experienced. Known for his deep understanding of game mechanics and player psychology, Brevik’s opinion carries significant weight in the gaming community. While he didn't name the specific game, his critique focuses on endings that feel unearned, cheapening the arduous journey players undertake. This sentiment echoes a broader discussion within the gaming world about the importance of satisfying conclusions that respect the player's time and investment.

Brevik’s own career is marked by a dedication to crafting engaging experiences, from the early days of **The Oregon Trail** and **Wizardry** on the Apple II to the monumental success of **Diablo** and **Diablo II**. He co-founded Condor, which became Blizzard North, and was instrumental in shaping the ARPG genre. His subsequent work on **Marvel Heroes** and **It Lurks Below**, as well as his current role at Skystone Games, demonstrates a continuous passion for game development. However, even a master craftsman like Brevik can find fault with how some games conclude their narratives, suggesting that the industry still has lessons to learn about delivering meaningful finales.

## The Cost of Always-Online and Rushed Endings

Brevik's criticism of rushed endings is particularly poignant given his insights into modern game development. He has previously expressed concerns that many contemporary ARPGs, including titles like **Path of Exile 2** and **Diablo 4**, often prioritize getting players to the endgame content as quickly as possible. This approach, he argues, "cheapens the entire experience." A significant factor he points to is the prevalence of "always online" game services, which can foster a culture of chasing "dopamine hits" rather than genuine fun and narrative satisfaction. This design philosophy, he believes, can detract from the immersive journey that makes a game truly memorable.

Furthermore, Brevik has been candid about the demanding nature of game development, even referencing the intense "crunch" culture during **Diablo II**'s development, which took a personal toll. This firsthand experience likely informs his perspective on how game design decisions, especially those aimed at maximizing player engagement through constant online interaction and rapid endgame access, can ultimately detract from the holistic player experience and the critical element of a satisfying conclusion. The desire for a well-crafted narrative arc, from beginning to end, remains a core tenet for many players and developers alike.

## What's Next

While **David Brevik** did not reveal the specific game with the offending ending, his comments serve as a potent reminder for developers to focus on the complete player journey. Players eager for more insights from the **Diablo** creator can anticipate future discussions as he continues his work at Skystone Games, potentially shaping the next generation of engaging interactive experiences.

content_raw: Disk Cleanup (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?" David Brevik's gaming history began before the arrival of the IBM PC. The veteran designer grew up playing games like Lode Runner and The Oregon Trail on the Apple II. "One that comes to mind right away is the original Wizardry ," Brevik says. "That had a huge impact on me. That was on the Apple II Plus, and I loved that game." Studying computer science at college, Brevik worked at numerous software and games companies before cofounding Condor, where he designed games like NFL Quarterback Club and Justice League Task Force. It was with Condor that Brevik pitched Diablo to then-publishers Blizzard Entertainment. After Blizzard acquired Condor and the studio was renamed Blizzard North, Diablo was released with the expectation of modest sales. Instead, the ARPG would become one of the most influential games of all time. Brevik left Blizzard in 2003 and has since designed games like Marvel Heroes and It Lurks Below . Today, Brevik is President of Skystone Games, which has published games such as Tiny Bookshop and Mistfall Hunter . But he took a break from searching for the next big hit to guide me through the isometric dungeon of his Steam library. What game are you currently playing? Strangely, a game that I'm playing the most recently is an old game of mine. I made this game called Marvel Heroes, which was in the 2010-12 range, and it's an ARPG with the Marvel superheroes. I originally went to that company to be the creative director, but over a period of a few years I became the CEO of the company, so I barely worked on the game for a while. I had to hire another replacement creative director, but I was still very involved in the project. Eventually I left the company. Being a CEO was basically raising money. I like making games. The point was, not long after I left, the company went out of business and the game shut down. It was a game that I spent many years of my career working on, and nobody could ever play it again. Along came some die-hard fans who ended up making their own server for the client, and they resurrected the game. So I've been playing this resurrected version of Marvel Heroes on this fan-made server. That's been really fun. Mainly I've been doing it a lot with the community. I was very involved with the community when I was playing. Made a lot of great friends, and I would stream the game almost every night. It was a little weird because, after I left, they changed the game. They had one more giant update that changed Marvel Heroes [from] the way it was originally designed.
